Starting a new job is exciting, and it's completely normal to feel anxious about it. Nearly everyone who has ever started somewhere new has felt the same knot in their stomach, and most of them were just as unsure of themselves as you are right now.

Try to remember that your employer hired you for a reason. They saw something in your application and interview that made them want you on the team. You don't have to prove that again on day one. Your only real job this week is to learn.

Prepare what you can ahead of time. Know the route and the start time, pack the night before, and write down a few questions you want to ask. Then let the rest go.

Once you're there, ask questions freely. People expect newcomers to be curious, and asking "Can you show me how that works?" is far better than guessing and getting it wrong. Take notes, because nobody remembers everything after the first day. Introduce yourself to people, even briefly, and try to learn a few names.

Be patient with yourself. You will probably feel lost at times, make small mistakes, and wonder if you chose wrong. That's part of the process, not evidence that you don't belong.

Finally, take care of your basics: eat properly, get some sleep, and give yourself something enjoyable to look forward to at the end of each day. A new job is a marathon, and the first week is just the warm-up.

**Review: Aurelia Pulse ANC Wireless Headphones ($129)**

The Aurelia Pulse is one of the most balanced options in the mid-range wireless headphone market, delivering solid sound, comfortable all-day wear, and useful features without the premium price tag.

Sound quality is the highlight. The 40mm drivers produce a warm, well-defined audio profile with punchy bass that doesn't muddy the mids. Vocals sound clear, and the treble stays crisp without becoming harsh. A companion app offers a graphic equalizer for tweaking the sound to your taste.

Active noise cancellation is effective against steady sounds like airplane engines and HVAC hum, though it struggles somewhat with sudden noises such as voices in an open office. Transparency mode is natural-sounding and useful for quick conversations.

Comfort is excellent. The memory foam earcups and lightweight frame (265 grams) made wearing them for several hours painless, though the headband can feel tight during the first few days.

Battery life is rated at 35 hours with ANC on, and in my testing I consistently got around 30. Multipoint Bluetooth lets you switch between a laptop and phone seamlessly, and a 10-minute quick charge provides roughly five hours of playback.

Call quality is decent in quiet settings but drops off in windy or crowded environments.

At $129, the Aurelia Pulse offers strong value. It isn't class-leading in noise cancellation or call clarity, but for everyday listening it's a reliable, comfortable choice. **Rating: 4/5**

**Solitude and Loneliness**

For years I believed that being alone and being lonely were the same thing. Both meant an empty room, a phone that didn't ring, a Saturday with no plans. It took me a long time to see that they only look alike from the outside.

Loneliness, I have come to understand, is a kind of hunger. It is the ache of wanting connection and not having it, and it tends to make time feel heavy. In lonely hours I watch the clock, rehearse old conversations, and wonder whether anyone would notice if I disappeared. The silence feels like an accusation.

Solitude is different. It is chosen, or at least embraced, and it has a texture of fullness rather than absence. I think of mornings spent with a notebook and a cooling cup of tea, or long walks where my thoughts rearranged themselves without anyone asking for an answer. In solitude the silence feels like space, something I can move through and even enjoy.

The difference, I suspect, lies less in circumstance than in relationship. A person can be surrounded by people and feel desperately alone, while another can spend a week in a cabin and feel perfectly whole. What matters is whether we are at peace with ourselves in the quiet.

I am still learning to tell the two apart in the moment, when the silence first arrives. But I have noticed that solitude tends to leave me more myself, and loneliness leaves me waiting for someone else to make me whole. Recognizing that difference has been its own quiet gift.

**City Council Approves Downtown Bike Lane Expansion**

The City Council voted 6-1 on Tuesday to approve a plan that will add 4.2 miles of protected bike lanes to the downtown core, with construction expected to begin next spring and wrap up within 18 months.

The expansion will extend existing lanes along Main Street and Fifth Avenue and connect them to the riverfront trail system. Council members said the project is designed to reduce traffic congestion, improve safety for cyclists and pedestrians, and give residents more transportation options.

"This is about making downtown easier to reach without a car," said Councilmember Dana Ruiz, who sponsored the measure. "We've heard from families, commuters, and small business owners who want safer streets."

Opposition came from Councilmember Tom Hartley, who voted against the plan over concerns about the loss of about 60 on-street parking spaces. Several downtown merchants also raised questions about delivery access during construction.

The city will hold a public open house next month to share detailed route maps and a construction schedule. Residents can also submit comments through the city's website.

The total cost of the project is estimated at $6.8 million, funded through a combination of state transportation grants and municipal capital funds.

Coffee's bitterness comes mainly from a group of compounds that act on our taste receptors in ways we've evolved to notice. Bitterness is a warning signal: many plant toxins taste bitter, so our ancestors learned to be wary of it.

Several compounds contribute. Chlorogenic acids, abundant in green coffee beans, break down during roasting into smaller molecules such as quinic acid and various lactones, which are sharply bitter. Caffeine itself is also bitter, though less so than many people assume; it contributes a modest share of the flavor. Roasting creates additional bitter compounds, including some from the browning reactions that give coffee its color and aroma.

Our tongues detect bitterness through receptors called TAS2Rs, a family of about 25 types in humans. Each responds to different bitter molecules, and together they let us sense a wide range of them. When a bitter compound binds to these receptors, it triggers signals that the brain interprets as "bitter."

Bitterness varies a lot with how coffee is made. Darker roasts often taste more bitter because roasting produces more of these compounds. Over-extraction, such as brewing too long or using water that is too hot, pulls out more bitter material than desirable. Lighter roasts and carefully controlled brewing tend to highlight acidity and sweetness instead.

Interestingly, bitterness is also a matter of perception. Genetics affect how sensitive people are to certain bitter compounds, and experience matters too, which is why many people come to enjoy coffee's bitterness over time.

**The Quiet Remaking of Our Cities**

Walk down a commercial street on a Tuesday afternoon and notice who is there. The lunch crowd is thinner than it used to be. The coffee shop has a line, but the people in it are wearing sweatpants and holding laptops. The dry cleaner is busier on weekdays, the gym has shifted its peak hours, and the nail salon down the block now books appointments at eleven in the morning. Nobody held a referendum on this. Remote work simply rearranged the city while most of us were busy adjusting to our kitchen tables.

The changes are real, even if they're easy to miss. Downtown office districts, built on the assumption that workers would arrive at nine and leave at six, are struggling with vacancy rates that would have been unthinkable a few years ago. Meanwhile, neighborhoods once treated as bedroom communities have become places where people work, shop, and spend their days. The residential street has become the workplace.

This matters because cities are not just economic machines. They are arrangements of shared time. When everyone commuted to the same towers, the streets had a rhythm: a morning surge, an evening exodus, a shared pulse. That rhythm supported restaurants, transit, and the small businesses that depend on predictable crowds. Remote work dissolved the rhythm into a scattered hum.

Some of this is wonderful. Parents are home for lunch. Commutes that ate two hours a day have vanished. But we should be honest that cities designed around the office are now guessing at their own purpose. Planners, shop owners, and transit agencies are all improvising. The question isn't whether remote work stays. It's whether we notice the city it has already built, and decide deliberately what kind of city we want it to be.

Here's a simple method for tying a classic four-in-hand knot:

1. **Start with the setup.** Drape the tie around your neck with the wide end about 12 inches lower than the narrow end. The narrow end should reach roughly the middle of your belt buckle.

2. **Cross the wide end over the narrow end.** Hold the narrow end still with your left hand (reverse these if you're left-handed).

3. **Wrap the wide end behind the narrow end.** Bring it around from right to left, going behind the narrow end.

4. **Bring the wide end up through the neck loop.** Pull it up through the opening between your neck and the knot.

5. **Cross the wide end down over the front.** Bring it across the front from left to right.

6. **Pass the wide end behind again.** Wrap it around behind the narrow end from right to left.

7. **Feed the wide end up through the front loop.** Push it up through the knot's front opening, from underneath.

8. **Tighten the knot.** Hold the front of the knot with one hand and slide it up to your collar by pulling the wide end downward gently.

9. **Adjust and finish.** Make sure the narrow end is hidden behind the wide end, and adjust the length so the tip of the wide end just reaches your belt buckle.

The bus sighed to a stop at the edge of Harrow's Crossing just as the light was going out of the sky. The door folded open with a hiss, and Ada Lind stepped down onto gravel, one hand on the strap of her canvas bag, the other shading her eyes against a sun that had already slipped behind the water tower.

Nobody else got off. The driver didn't look back at her. He pulled away with a shudder of diesel, and the red of his taillights dwindled down the county road until the dark swallowed them.

She stood alone in front of a single-bay shelter with a bench and a faded schedule taped to its glass. The schedule had been wrong, she suspected, for years.

Harrow's Crossing was smaller than she remembered, or maybe she had only remembered it bigger because she'd been a child when she left. A grain elevator. A diner with one window lit and a neon coffee cup flickering in the glass. A row of houses with porch lights coming on one by one, as if someone were walking the street and touching each switch.

Ada shifted the bag higher on her shoulder. Her boots were wrong for this. Her coat was wrong for this. Everything about her was city-thin and out of place, and she felt it on her skin like the cooling air.

Across the road, a man in a feed cap leaned against the diner's doorframe. He wasn't watching her exactly. He was watching the bus route, the empty stretch of asphalt where the taillights had been, as though he expected something else to come down it.

Then he looked at her, and his face changed, slowly, the way a closed door might open.

"Well," he said, not loudly. "You came back."

Ada opened her mouth to tell him he was mistaken, and found she couldn't quite say it.

HTTPS is HTTP wrapped inside TLS (Transport Layer Security), and TLS protects a request in three main ways: it hides the content, verifies who you're talking to, and detects tampering.

**1. Encryption.** Before any web data is sent, the browser and server perform a TLS handshake. They agree on keys using asymmetric cryptography (the server proves ownership of its public key, and the two sides derive a shared secret without ever sending it in the clear). From then on, everything is encrypted with fast symmetric encryption using that shared key. Anyone sniffing the network sees only scrambled bytes: the URL path, headers, cookies, and body are all unreadable. They can still see the destination IP address and, usually, the domain name via SNI, but not what you're asking for.

**2. Authentication.** Encryption alone isn't enough, because you could be encrypting to an attacker. The server presents a certificate signed by a Certificate Authority (CA) that your browser trusts. The certificate binds a domain name to a public key. If the name doesn't match or the chain of signatures doesn't verify, the browser refuses the connection.

**3. Integrity.** Each encrypted record carries a message authentication code. If an attacker alters even one bit in transit, the receiver detects the mismatch and drops the connection.

In short: the handshake establishes a secret only the two endpoints know, the certificate proves the server's identity, and the cipher plus MAC keeps the traffic private and unmodified.

1/5 We launched a product last year that flopped. Six months of work, a big launch day, and almost no sales. Here's the hard lesson it taught me, and why I'd do it differently now.

2/5 We built for three months before talking to a single customer. We were sure we knew the problem. We didn't. When we finally showed people the product, the first question was "Why would I switch from what I already use?" We had no good answer.

3/5 The lesson: validate demand before you build, not after. Get people to pay, or at least commit, before you write production code. A landing page, a waitlist with real emails, or pre-orders will tell you more in two weeks than a year of internal planning.

4/5 We also confused a launch with a strategy. We spent our budget on one big day instead of a steady stream of small tests. When the day came and went quietly, we had nothing to fall back on. Launches are announcements. They don't create demand on their own.

5/5 Now my rule is simple: if I can't name five specific people who would be disappointed if this product disappeared, I don't build it yet. The failure cost us money and months, but it taught me more about my customers than any success did.

Listen up. First week at a new job, you're going to feel like you're drowning. That's normal. Everybody on this line felt it, including the guy who's been here ten years.

Here's what you do. Show up early. Not on time, early. Learn where the walk-in is, where the towels are, where the fire extinguisher hangs. Nobody expects you to know the menu cold by Tuesday.

Ask questions. Ask them when you're unsure, not after you've screwed up the sauce. A question takes ten seconds. A burned batch takes an hour and everybody's mad.

Write stuff down. Prep lists, recipe quirks, who likes their steak how. Nobody's impressed by memory, they're impressed by someone who doesn't make the same mistake twice.

Keep your station clean and your mouth shut when you don't know something. Watch what the others do. Copy the good habits.

And stop catastrophizing at 2 a.m. You're not getting fired for being new. You get fired for being careless or rude. Be neither, and you'll be fine.

Now get some sleep. Your first shift's in the morning.

**TO THE CITIZENS OF EVERY CITY, AWAKE!**

Hear me, you who still believe the downtown towers are the beating heart of commerce! While you were distracted by the clamor of return-to-office edicts, a quiet revolution has crept through our streets, and no proclamation announced it.

Consider the lunch counter that now sits empty at noon. Consider the dry cleaner, the barber, the bookshop, the sandwich man whose trade once depended on clerks trudging forth at the stroke of twelve. Their customers have not vanished. They have simply moved into the neighborhoods, into the kitchens, into the coffee shops of quiet avenues where rents were once the province of artists and the old and the poor.

And what of the landlord? He grows fat on the new arrangement, raising rents where the remote worker has come to stay, while the bus lines that once carried thousands to their desks now rumble through half-empty and forlorn. The city, which was built for the crowd, must now serve the solitary laptop, and it does so badly.

Do not mistake this for mere convenience. It is a reshuffling of wealth, of power, of who may afford to live where the life of a town is made. The office once concentrated money in one district. Now it scatters it across a hundred neighborhoods, and yet the tax rolls, the transit budgets, and the zoning boards still speak the old language of the empty center.

Rise, then, reformers! Remake the city for those who inhabit it by day as well as by night. The old downtown does not die; it is merely waiting for your wisdom.

Feeling anxious before your first week at a new job is normal. You’re stepping into unfamiliar routines, meeting new people, and learning what’s expected—all at once. You don’t need to prove yourself immediately. Your main job this week is to learn, connect, and settle in.

A few things can help:

- **Make the basics easier.** Plan your commute, choose comfortable clothes, and check your start time. Reducing small uncertainties can make the day feel more manageable.
- **Take notes and ask questions.** Nobody expects you to know everything. Write down names, processes, and unfamiliar terms, and ask which tasks deserve your attention first.
- **Aim for connection, not perfection.** Introduce yourself, join a conversation, or ask a colleague how they got started. Small, friendly moments count.
- **Give yourself recovery time.** A new environment can be tiring, even when things go well. Keep evenings simple and protect your sleep.

When anxiety spikes, pause, take a slow breath, and focus on the next manageable step rather than the whole week.

At the end of each day, notice one thing you learned and one thing that went okay. Progress may feel awkward before it feels comfortable. Being new is a temporary stage—not a test you have to ace.

Coffee tastes bitter because its beans contain compounds that activate **bitter-taste receptors** on your tongue. Caffeine is one of them, but it’s not the main source of bitterness in a typical cup—even decaf can taste quite bitter.

Much of coffee’s bitterness develops during **roasting**. Green coffee beans contain chlorogenic acids, which break down and transform as the beans heat up. Medium roasting produces compounds called chlorogenic acid lactones, which contribute a relatively mild bitterness. Darker roasting creates more phenylindanes, associated with a stronger, more lingering bitterness. That’s one reason a dark roast often tastes harsher than a lighter one.

Brewing matters, too. Hot water dissolves substances from ground coffee, and the balance changes with temperature, grind size, and contact time. When extraction goes too far, the resulting cup can taste disproportionately bitter or drying. But bitterness and drying astringency are different sensations, even though people often lump them together.

Your perception also depends on the rest of the cup: sweetness can soften bitterness, while coffee’s aromas and acidity shape how balanced it tastes. People vary in their sensitivity to bitter compounds, too.

So bitterness isn’t necessarily a flaw—it’s a natural part of coffee’s flavor. The goal is balance, not its complete removal.

### How to Tie a Necktie: The Four-in-Hand Knot

This simple, slightly asymmetrical knot works well with most ties and shirt collars. Directions refer to your own left and right.

1. **Position the tie.** Raise your collar and drape the tie around your neck, with the wide end on your right and the narrow end on your left. Let the wide end hang about 12 inches lower than the narrow end.

2. **Cross the ends.** Bring the wide end across the front of the narrow end, moving from right to left.

3. **Wrap underneath.** Pass the wide end behind the narrow end, bringing it back to your right.

4. **Cross again.** Bring the wide end across the front once more, moving toward your left. Keep this front band slightly loose.

5. **Go through the neck loop.** Feed the wide end upward through the loop between your tie and your neck.

6. **Thread the front.** Bring the wide end down through the loose front band.

7. **Tighten and adjust.** Hold the narrow end and slide the knot upward. Straighten it, lower your collar, and check that the wide tip reaches your belt buckle.

HTTPS is HTTP carried over **TLS (Transport Layer Security)**. It keeps a web request private by encrypting traffic between your client and the server handling the HTTPS connection.

Before sending HTTP data, the client and server perform a **TLS handshake**:

1. **Verify the server’s identity.** The server presents a certificate for its domain. Your browser checks that the certificate is valid, matches the hostname, and chains back to a trusted certificate authority. This helps prevent an attacker from impersonating the site.
2. **Establish shared keys.** Using a key-exchange protocol, the client and server derive shared encryption keys without sending those keys across the network.
3. **Protect application data.** They use those keys to encrypt and authenticate HTTP traffic. Someone monitoring the network cannot read the URL path, query parameters, headers, cookies, or request body. Tampering is also detected.

HTTPS does **not** hide everything. Observers can still see the destination IP address, connection timing, and approximate traffic size. The domain may also be visible through DNS or TLS metadata, depending on which privacy features are used.

Finally, encryption ends wherever TLS terminates—possibly at a CDN or load balancer. HTTPS protects data **in transit**, not from the receiving service itself or from a compromised client or server.

To the outside observer, solitude and loneliness look remarkably the same. Both involve a person sitting alone in a quiet room, walking solo through a park, or dining at a table for one. Yet, beneath the surface, these two states of being are worlds apart. The difference does not lie in our physical surroundings, but in our internal landscape. 

Loneliness is Marked by a sense of lack. It is an involuntary ache, a hollow space within us that craves the presence of others to feel whole. Ironically, loneliness does not always require physical isolation; it can strike just as sharply in a crowded room when we feel unseen or misunderstood. It is a barren state where silence feels heavy and oppressive, acting as a reminder of our disconnection from the world.

Solitude, on the other hand, is a state of fullness. It is the conscious choice to step away from the noise of the world not to escape others, but to find oneself. In solitude, silence is not an absence, but a comforting presence. It is the fertile ground where creativity blooms, exhausted minds recharge, and deep self-reflection occurs. When we are in solitude, we are not truly alone; we are simply in our own company, and we find that company to be enough.

Ultimately, the bridge between loneliness and solitude is self-acceptance. When we learn to be a gentle, welcoming host to our own thoughts, the dread of being alone evaporates. Loneliness is the poverty of self; solitude is the richness of it.

When you take a sip of coffee, that signature bite is actually an evolutionary defense mechanism. Coffee beans are the seeds of a fruit, and the coffee plant produces bitter compounds as natural pesticides to deter insects and foraging animals.

You might assume caffeine is the main culprit. While caffeine is undeniably bitter, it accounts for only about 10% to 15% of coffee’s bitterness. The real stars of the show are **chlorogenic acids**—antioxidants packed into raw coffee beans—and the alchemy of roasting. 

When green coffee beans are exposed to high heat, chlorogenic acids break down into **chlorogenic acid lactones**, which yield a pleasant, mild bitterness found in light and medium roasts. If the beans are roasted longer and hotter to create a dark roast, these lactones break down further into **phenylindanes**. These compounds carry a much harsher, lingering bitterness, explaining why an espresso roast bites harder than a blonde roast, even though both come from the same bean.

Finally, how you brew matters. Bitterness is the last flavor extracted by hot water. If you use water that is too hot, grind your beans too finely, or steep them too long, you pull out an excess of these heavy compounds, resulting in an over-extracted, overly bitter cup.

For years, urban theorists predicted that remote work would trigger an "urban doom loop," leaving cities hollowed out and obsolete. That dramatic apocalypse never arrived. Instead, remote work has executed a quieter, far more fascinating revolution: it hasn’t killed the city; it has decentralized it.

Historically, cities operated like giant lungs, inhaling commuters into gleaming central business districts at 9 a.m. and exhaling them back to the suburbs at 5 p.m. Today, that rhythm is broken. While downtown office towers still struggle with stubbornly high vacancies, the surrounding residential neighborhoods are experiencing a renaissance. 

Walk through a formerly sleepy outer-ring neighborhood on a Tuesday afternoon, and you will see the new urban economy in action. Laptop-toting workers fill local bakeries; dog walkers crowd neighborhood parks at midday; dry cleaners and bodegas near apartment buildings are thriving, while those near central transit hubs wither. The economic vitality of the metropolis hasn't vanished—it has simply migrated a few miles away from the skyscrapers. 

Even time itself has been reshaped. The rigid five-day rush hour has softened, replaced by a "Tuesday-to-Thursday" downtown pulse, while Fridays now blend seamlessly into the weekend. 

Remote work didn’t destroy urban life; it localized it. To thrive in this new era, city leaders must stop mourning the 2019 commuter and start investing in the vibrant, 15-minute neighborhoods where modern life actually happens.

Here is how to tie a classic Four-in-Hand knot, the easiest and most versatile way to wear a necktie. 

**Step 1: The Setup**
Flip your shirt collar up and drape the tie around your neck. Position the wide end on your dominant side and the narrow end on the other. The wide end should hang about 12 inches lower than the narrow end. Throughout this process, you will only be moving the wide end.

**Step 2: The Wrap**
Cross the wide end horizontally over the front of the narrow end. Next, wrap the wide end horizontally behind the narrow end. 

**Step 3: The Knot**
Bring the wide end back across the front from left to right. This creates the smooth front face of your knot, so keep the fabric flat.

**Step 4: The Loop**
Pull the wide end up and through the loop around your neck from underneath. 

**Step 5: The Finish**
Tuck the wide end down through the front knot you created in Step 3. Hold the narrow end with one hand and use the other to slide the knot up to your collar. Fold your collar down, adjust the tightness, and you are ready to go!

At its core, HTTPS is just standard HTTP wrapped inside an encrypted tunnel called **TLS (Transport Layer Security)**. While standard HTTP sends data in plaintext over TCP—allowing anyone on the network to read it—HTTPS scrambles the data before it ever leaves the client. 

Here is how it establishes privacy, right after the standard TCP three-way handshake:

**1. The TLS Handshake (Asymmetric Encryption):** 
The server sends the client its SSL/TLS Certificate, which contains a **public key**. The client verifies this certificate with a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) to ensure the server isn't an imposter. Using the server's public key, the client and server securely negotiate a new, temporary **session key**. 

**2. The Data Transfer (Symmetric Encryption):**
Asymmetric encryption is mathematically heavy, so it's only used for the handshake. Once both sides have the shared session key, they switch to **symmetric encryption** (like AES). Now, your entire HTTP request—headers, URL paths, cookies, and JSON payloads—is encrypted using this session key before being broken into TCP packets.

**What the network sees:**
Because encryption happens *below* the HTTP layer, routers and hackers sniffing the network can still see the IP addresses and ports (Layer 3/4), and usually the base domain name (via SNI). However, the actual HTTP request and response look like pure gibberish.

**The Quiet Divide: Solitude vs. Loneliness**

Though often used interchangeably, solitude and loneliness are fundamentally different states of being. The distinction lies not in whether one is alone, but in the internal relationship one has with that stillness.

Loneliness is a state of deficiency. It is a heavy, aching void characterized by a sense of isolation and the longing for connection. It is not defined by the absence of people, but by the absence of *feeling seen*. One can be in a crowded room or a lifelong marriage and still feel profoundly lonely if there is a disconnect between their inner world and their external environment. Loneliness is a hunger—a painful reminder of the human need to belong.

Solitude, conversely, is a state of abundance. It is the intentional act of stepping away from the noise of the world to reconnect with the self. In solitude, being alone is a choice and a sanctuary. It is the space where creativity flourishes, where reflection deepens, and where the soul recovers from the exhaustion of social performance. While loneliness is a burden to be escaped, solitude is a gift to be cultivated.

Ultimately, the difference is a matter of perspective. Loneliness is the fear of being alone; solitude is the joy of it. When we transform our loneliness into solitude, we cease to be victims of our isolation and instead become architects of our own inner peace.

The bitter taste of coffee is a complex phenomenon attributed to a combination of factors. Coffee beans contain a group of compounds called alkaloids, particularly caffeine, which is a major contributor to bitterness. When coffee is roasted, the heat breaks down some of these compounds, but also creates new ones through a process called the Maillard reaction. This reaction involves the interaction of amino acids and sugars, resulting in the formation of new flavor compounds, some of which are bitter.

Additionally, coffee contains a class of compounds called polyphenols, which are known to contribute to bitterness and astringency. Chlorogenic acids, a type of polyphenol, are particularly prevalent in coffee and are responsible for some of its bitter taste.

The brewing method can also impact the perceived bitterness of coffee. Factors such as water temperature, brewing time, and coffee-to-water ratio can influence the extraction of bitter compounds from the coffee grounds. For example, a higher water temperature or longer brewing time can result in a more bitter taste.

Overall, the bitter taste of coffee is a result of the combination of naturally occurring compounds in the coffee beans, the roasting process, and the brewing method. This complex interplay of factors contributes to the characteristic bitterness that many coffee lovers have come to appreciate.

Here are step-by-step instructions for tying a **Four-In-Hand knot**, the most classic and versatile necktie knot.

**Preparation:**
Drape the tie around your neck. Position the wide end on your right and the narrow end on your left. The narrow end should sit just above your belt line.

**Steps:**
1. **The Cross:** Cross the wide end over the narrow end.
2. **The Wrap:** Bring the wide end underneath the narrow end, passing it to the right.
3. **The Over:** Bring the wide end back across the front, moving from right to left. This creates a horizontal loop.
4. **The Loop:** Pull the wide end up through the neck loop (the space between the tie and your collar).
5. **The Finish:** Tuck the wide end down through the horizontal loop you just created in Step 3.
6. **Tighten:** Hold the narrow end and gently slide the knot upward toward your collar. 

**Pro Tip:** Ensure the tip of the wide end rests exactly at the center of your belt buckle for a polished look.

HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) ensures privacy by layering HTTP inside a security protocol called **TLS (Transport Layer Security)**. It achieves this through a two-step process: the **Handshake** and **Symmetric Encryption**.

### 1. The Handshake (Asymmetric Encryption)
When you connect to a server, they perform a "handshake." The server sends its **Public Key** and a **Digital Certificate** (signed by a trusted Certificate Authority). Your browser verifies the certificate to ensure the server is who it claims to be. 

Using that public key, your browser encrypts a random "session key" and sends it back. Because only the server possesses the corresponding **Private Key**, only the server can decrypt it. This solves the "key exchange problem"—sharing a secret key over an insecure channel.

### 2. Data Transfer (Symmetric Encryption)
Now that both sides have the same shared session key, they switch to **Symmetric Encryption**. This is much faster than asymmetric encryption. Every single byte of data (URLs, cookies, form data) is encrypted using this key before leaving the device.

**In short:** Asymmetric encryption is used to securely agree on a secret key, and symmetric encryption uses that key to keep the actual data private from eavesdroppers.

Solitude and loneliness can look alike from the outside: a person alone, a quiet room, an evening without company. Inside, they are different climates.

Solitude is chosen, or at least accepted. It is the space in which attention returns to itself—where a walk becomes thinking, and silence becomes room enough to hear one’s own mind. In solitude, absence is not a wound; it is a margin. People seek it to read, to grieve cleanly, to pray, to make something, or simply to rest from the performance of being with others. The self is not missing; it is present without an audience.

Loneliness is the ache of wanting connection and not finding it. It can arrive in a crowd as easily as in an empty house, because it is not measured by the number of bodies nearby but by the feeling of being unseen. Time stretches. Small rejections loom. The mind rehearses conversations that never happen. Loneliness is not a virtue or a failure; it is a signal that belonging has thinned.

The difference, then, is not whether one is alone, but whether aloneness feels like shelter or exile. Solitude can restore; loneliness depletes. One may even hold both in the same hour—grateful for quiet, and still wishing someone would call. Knowing the difference matters. It lets us protect the solitude we need, and answer the loneliness we should not have to carry alone.

Coffee tastes bitter mainly because of compounds created when coffee beans are roasted, not because of caffeine alone.

Raw beans are seeds full of sugars, proteins, acids, and chlorogenic acids. Heat breaks those down and rearranges them. Chlorogenic acids split into caffeic and quinic acids, which taste sharp and bitter. Sugars and amino acids also undergo Maillard reactions and caramelization, producing brown pigments and a large family of bitter-tasting molecules. Darker roasts push these reactions further, so they often taste more bitter and less acidic than lighter roasts, even though they contain slightly less caffeine.

Caffeine does contribute a clean, lingering bitterness, but it is only part of the story. Brewing extracts whatever is soluble. Hotter water, finer grounds, and longer contact pull out more of the bitter compounds along with desirable aromas. Over-extraction is why a pot left on the burner, or espresso pulled too long, can taste harsh.

Your tongue detects these molecules with bitter receptors, an ancient warning system for potentially toxic plant chemicals. Coffee’s bitterness is balanced by aroma, sweetness from caramelized sugars, acidity, and fats in the brew. Milk, sugar, or a slightly coarser grind and shorter brew can soften it without removing the compounds that make coffee taste like coffee.

Remote work did not empty the city so much as rewrite it. The change arrived without a parade: fewer morning crushes, quieter lunch lines, and offices that still look occupied from the street while half their desks stay dark. What used to be a five-day ritual is now a negotiated presence.

That shift has consequences cities are only beginning to admit. Downtowns built on the assumption that hundreds of thousands of people would arrive, spend, and leave by evening are discovering that “sometimes” is a weak foundation for a commercial district. Coffee shops near transit hubs feel it first. So do dry cleaners, lunch counters, and the small retailers that lived off the weekday crowd. Tax bases tied to office occupancy look less certain when leases shrink and companies treat headquarters as a gathering place rather than a daily requirement.

But the story is not only loss. Neighborhoods that were dormitories between commutes have become places where people actually spend the day. Side streets have more foot traffic at 11 a.m. Libraries, parks, and corner cafés absorb work that used to happen twenty miles away. The city is less a machine for moving bodies to a center and more a patchwork of local routines.

Planners still talk as if the old pattern will snap back. It will not, not fully. Remote work has quietly moved demand from the core to the edges, from lunch hours to irregular days, from spectacle to ordinary life. Cities that notice will redesign around that. Cities that don’t will keep waiting for a rush hour that no longer comes.

Tying a Four-in-Hand necktie is straightforward.

1. Button your collar and raise it. Drape the tie around your neck with the wide end on your right, hanging about 12 inches lower than the narrow end on your left.
2. Cross the wide end over the narrow end, then bring it underneath and back to the right so the wide end lies across the front again.
3. Wrap the wide end horizontally across the front of the narrow end, moving from right to left.
4. Bring the wide end up through the loop between your collar and the tie, from underneath.
5. Pass the wide end down through the front knot you just formed. Do not pull it all the way through yet.
6. Hold the narrow end and gently slide the knot upward, tightening as you go. Keep the knot centered and the dimple neat.
7. Adjust the length so the tip of the wide end meets the top of your belt buckle. Fold the collar down.

If the tip is too short or too long, loosen the knot and start again with a different starting length. Practice a few times; the motion becomes automatic.

HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS, so the request and response are encrypted on the wire instead of sent as plain text.

Before any HTTP bytes are exchanged, the client and server run a TLS handshake. The server presents a certificate that chains to a trusted certificate authority. The client checks that the certificate is valid and that its name matches the host it intended to reach. That step authenticates the server, so a network attacker cannot simply impersonate the site and read the traffic.

During the handshake they also agree on a cipher suite and derive shared session keys. Modern TLS uses ephemeral key exchange (typically ECDHE), so those keys are unique to the connection and are not recoverable later even if the server’s long-term private key leaks. After the handshake, HTTP—including the URL path, headers, and body—is encrypted with those keys. Anyone who only sees the packets gets ciphertext, not the request contents. TLS also adds integrity checks (MAC or AEAD), so tampering is detected and the connection fails closed.

What remains visible to the network is mostly metadata: IP addresses, the destination port (usually 443), and, with older TLS or without Encrypted Client Hello, the server name in SNI. The contents of the web request itself stay private between the client and the authenticated server.

Citizens, mark well what has befallen your cities while you were busy congratulating yourselves upon convenience. The counting-house has fled the street. The clerk no longer crowds the omnibus at dawn, nor spends his coin at the tavern, the tailor, the stationer, the coffee-house that once lived upon his passing. Remote labor, that soft-footed usurper, has emptied the pavements without a riot and thinned the rents without a proclamation.

Be not deceived by the silence. A city is not a museum of towers; it is a bargain struck hourly among strangers. When the bargain is struck instead in the parlor, the shopkeeper starves, the landlord trembles, and the young, who once learned the world by jostling through it, learn only the glow of a screen. Downtown becomes a stage set: handsome, hollow, and kept alive by tourists and the few who still must appear in the flesh.

I do not mourn the commute as if it were a sacrament. I mourn the civic muscle that withers when men and women cease to share a street. Liberty was never meant to be practiced solely from an armchair. Coffee tastes bitter mainly because roasting creates bitter compounds and because humans are wired to detect them.

Raw coffee beans are not very bitter. During roasting, sugars and amino acids react in the Maillard reaction, producing dark, flavorful compounds—some bitter. Chlorogenic acids, natural antioxidants in beans, also transform into bitter lactones. Caffeine contributes bitterness too, though it’s only part of the story; decaf coffee can still taste bitter.

We perceive these compounds through TAS2R taste receptors on the tongue. There are about 25 types, and coffee activates several. Interestingly, bitterness sensitivity varies genetically: some people are “supertasters” for certain bitter molecules, so coffee may taste harsher to them.

Why would we evolve to taste bitterness? Many bitter plant compounds are toxic, so bitterness is a warning signal. Coffee’s bitterness isn’t dangerous, but our biology still flags it. Roast level, brewing method, water temperature, and grind size all change which bitter compounds end up in your cup. So coffee’s bitterness is a complex mix of chemistry and evolution—not just caffeine.

HTTPS is HTTP carried inside TLS. When your browser connects, it first does a TLS handshake. The server presents a certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority; the browser verifies it matches the domain, proving you’re talking to the real server, not an impostor.

Next, client and server use asymmetric cryptography (often ECDHE) to securely agree on a shared session key. That key is never sent directly over the network. Once established, the actual HTTP request and response are encrypted with fast symmetric encryption, such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. This means anyone in the middle—your Wi‑Fi router, ISP, or a proxy—sees only encrypted bytes, not URLs, headers, cookies, or form data. TLS also adds integrity checks, so attackers can’t silently modify the request.

So HTTPS gives confidentiality and integrity in transit: only your browser and the server can read or alter the request. It does not hide everything: observers may still see IP addresses, ports, timing, and sometimes the domain via SNI. But the request contents remain private.

The real culprits are **chlorogenic acids**, which are naturally abundant in raw coffee beans. When heat is applied during roasting, these acids break down into two key groups of compounds:

- **Chlorogenic acid lactones**, which form at lighter to medium roast levels and produce a pleasant, mild bitterness.
- **Phenylindanes**, which form at darker roast levels and deliver a harsher, more lingering bitterness.

This is why a light roast often tastes brighter and more acidic, while a dark roast tastes more aggressively bitter—the chemistry has shifted toward those phenylindanes.

Brewing also matters. Over-extraction (water too hot, contact time too long, grind too fine) pulls more of these bitter compounds into your cup. That's why a well-brewed coffee balances bitterness with sweetness and acidity, while a poorly brewed one can taste unpleasantly harsh.

In short: bitterness in coffee is mostly a product of heat transforming natural plant chemicals.

**How to Tie a Necktie (Four-in-Hand Knot)**

1. Drape the tie around your collar with the wide end on your right side, hanging about 12 inches lower than the narrow end.

2. Cross the wide end over the narrow end.

3. Bring the wide end underneath the narrow end, pulling it to the left.

4. Bring the wide end back across the front, moving from left to right.

5. Pull the wide end up through the loop around your neck.

6. Slide the wide end down through the knot you've just formed in front.

7. Gently tighten the knot by holding the narrow end and sliding the knot upward toward your collar.

8. Adjust the tie so the knot sits centered and the tip reaches your belt buckle.

For a polished finish, create a small dimple just below the knot by pinching the fabric as you tighten. Tuck the narrow end into the keeper loop on the back of the wide end.

## How HTTPS Keeps a Request Private

When you make a plain HTTP request, everything—headers, URL path, body—travels as readable text. Anyone on the network path (your ISP, a coffee shop router) can see it.

HTTPS wraps HTTP inside **TLS** (Transport Layer Security). Here's the short version of what happens:

**1. The TLS Handshake**
Your browser and the server agree on a shared secret. The server proves its identity with a certificate (signed by a trusted Certificate Authority), and both sides use asymmetric cryptography (public/private keys) to safely derive a symmetric session key.

**2. Symmetric Encryption**
Once both sides have that session key, they use it to encrypt all the actual HTTP data—headers, path, body. Symmetric encryption is fast, and only the two endpoints know the key.

**What stays private:** the URL path, query parameters, headers, and body.

**What's still visible:** the destination IP address and the domain name (via DNS and the TLS SNI field), plus timing and size of traffic.

So HTTPS doesn't hide *where* you're connecting, but it hides *what* you're saying.

The fix we should have made before launch:

Sit behind a real user for 30 minutes while they do their actual job. Not a guided tour. Not a curated scenario. Just watch them work.

You'll see every friction point your demo conveniently skipped.

Citizens! You have been robbed, and no man has cried alarm!

The great cities of our age—that mighty engine of commerce and communion—have been hollowed out not by plague, not by war, but by a revolution so quiet that its perpetrators did not even know they were revolutionaries. They simply closed their laptops and departed.

Behold the empty towers! Behold the sandwich shops shuttered, the shoe-shine men idle, the transit cars running half-empty like veins drained of blood. The landlord still demands his tribute, yet the tenant has fled to the provinces, there to labour from his parlour in his nightshirt, answerable to no clock but his own.

They call this "flexibility." I call it the dissolution of the social compact. A city is not a collection of buildings—it is the friction of bodies, the collision of minds, the very marketplace of civilization itself.

And now we are told this is progress? That we shall become atoms, each spinning alone in his little orbit, producing and consuming and perishing in isolation?

I say: a city abandoned is a republic abandoned. Wake, citizens, before you find you have no city at all.
